newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Maori activist takes sledgehammer to America's Cup.
newsitem.headline: Maori activist takes sledgehammer to America's Cup.

text.p: A man shouting Maori slogans attacked yachting's prestigious America's Cup with a sledgehammer on Friday and inflicted serious damage on the oldest trophy in sport, New Zealand police said.
Police spokeswoman Joanne Gibbs said a Maori man walked into the room where the cup was on display at the Royal New Zealand Yacht Squadron in Auckland.
She said the man, dressed in a suit, took a sledgehammer from a bag and rained blows on the glass cabinet containing the trophy, known as the Auld Mug.
"He then took off his suit to indicate that he had some sort of protest T-shirt underneath, shouted a few things and he was then held on to by people who where there," Gibbs said.
"I believe it was some sort of Maori activist protest," she told Reuters.
Maoris, the original Polynesian settlers of New Zealand, now make up about 13 percent of the population. A small group of fringe activists has led sporadic campaigns for Maori sovereignty.
The man, who has yet to be identified, was still being interviewed by police.
The cup, which is insured for an undisclosed sum, arrived in New Zealand to ticker tape parades in 1995 following Team New Zealand's victory over Dennis Conner's Stars and Stripes in San Diego.
It was one of this country's greatest sporting achievements, drawing comparisons with New Zealander Sir Edmund Hillary's conquest of Mount Everest in 1953.
The capture of the trophy, which in 144 years had only once before been wrested away from the United States, prompted an outpouring of national pride.
A spokeswoman for Prime Minister Jim Bolger said he was "disgusted" by the attack, while Sports Minister Murray McCully called it "a mindless act of a complete idiot".
Team New Zealand leader Sir Peter Blake, who was knighted for his efforts in securing the cup, said he was shocked.
"I'm a bit stunned to think that a New Zealander would want to demolish, try and demolish or steal or damage the America's Cup," he said.

John Heise, commodore of the Auckland club, said: "I think it is a blow not only for the yacht squadron but for the public of New Zealand, because we've taken the attitude that the cup is New Zealand's cup and not just the yacht squadron's cup."

Heise said it was likely the trophy would have to be completely remade from original drawings. He declined to put a value on the cup, but the the San Diego Yacht Club had it insured for US$2 million when it was in their possession.
New Zealand is due to defend the America's Cup in Auckland in the year 2000.
